text:
$IREN

IREN's EV is ~$13B. The two worries hitting the stock are Microsoft and Texas, so here are both, plus the power and pricing the market is valuing.

MICROSOFT
• Thursday, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is tightening oversight of neocloud projects at IREN, Nebius and Nscale and debating whether to sign new neocloud deals. IREN fell 17% to $18.03, Nebius ~15% and CoreWeave ~10%

• IREN's side: Microsoft asked for network design changes, some deliveries move into early 2027, and IREN says that carries no financial penalties. The data centers are "practically done" and waiting on equipment to finish commissioning

• The >$4B ARR target, fully contracted and funded, moves from year-end to January, possibly February. The stock rose 20% on Friday after the results

TEXAS
• Aug 3: Abbott paused approvals for data centers moving through ERCOT's interconnection process pending an audit. Sept 21: he told TCEQ to halt permits for data centers seeking new grid connections. ERCOT's report is due by Dec 10

• Nov 3: Gina Hinojosa was elected governor. She has said she would ban new data center projects until lawmakers pass rules for the industry. She takes office in January

• IREN's main Texas sites already have power. Sweetwater 1, 1.4GW, has been energized since May 1, and Childress hosts the Microsoft and NVIDIA contracts. Sweetwater 2 has a signed 600MW grid connection agreement, and both phases are in the base load of ERCOT's Batch Zero process

• Bernstein argued after Abbott's pause that it makes approved MWs more valuable. On Nov 4 it cut its target to $55 from $100 over the election and kept Outperform

THE POWER
• >5GW secured on 30,000+ acres: Sweetwater and Childress in Texas, Mackenzie in BC, where a new 100MW liquid-cooled build started, 300MW in Badajoz, Spain, targeting 2028, plus Kiowa in Oklahoma and Bundey in Australia

• ~$2.6M of EV per MW of secured power (my math). In Oct 2025 a consortium including BlackRock's GIP, MGX, Microsoft, NVIDIA and xAI agreed to buy Aligned Data Centers for ~$40B, ~$8M per MW of its ~5GW. Aligned runs ~50 data centers, so it isn't a clean comp, but IREN's power is priced at about a third of that

PRICING IS GOING UP
• Contracted pricing rose 11% on 3-year deals and 12% on 5-year deals

• H100s, a chip that started shipping in 2022, were contracted at double their original pricing, on long-term deals

• 3-year deals at $19-23M of annual revenue per IT MW, a new 5-year deal at ~$22M with ~90% of GPU capex prepaid, and a short-term deal above $40M

• The >$4B ARR program runs on 0.3GW of IT, ~$13M per IT MW (my math). GPU mix drives these numbers, but new deals are priced well above it

THE TRANSITION
• FY26: $707M of revenue, $578.2M mining and $128.8M AI cloud, ~18%

• Q1 FY27: $228M, AI cloud $200M, ~88%. AI cloud gross margin 86%. Adj. EBITDA $66M, up from $19M

• The CFO aims to substantially finish decommissioning the miners this quarter

FUNDING
~$6B of the $15B of remaining FY27 capex isn't committed yet. Management says that sits against $12-15B of potential sources before converts or equity, after raising $19B in the 12 months to September. Net debt rose from $216M to $4.43B in the quarter. Total debt is $10.2B, mostly low-coupon converts, and the Microsoft GPUs are financed with $3.6B of investment-grade debt at 6.0%. Management expects $25B of data center and GPU assets by June 2027.

Price targets as of Friday: Goldman $30, Jones $40 after an upgrade to Buy, Cantor $47, Bernstein $55, Northland $74. Goldman, Cantor, Bernstein and Northland all cut, and the lowest is still 39% above Friday's close.

text:
I’m skeptical about the utility of humanoids compared to task specific robots or cobots, based on strategic issues like ‘The Hand Problem’, short battery life, training complexity and unit cost. There  hasn’t been much real world data but now, some data is becoming available.

Agility Robotics' commercial deployments of its Digit humanoid robot and key performance indicators became public with the recent filing of its SEC S-4 (in this case a SPAC version of an S-1). Here they are:

1. Revenue-Generating Customers: Agility has deployed its Digit v4 units across 9 pilot customer sites (including Amazon, GXO Logistics, Schaeffler, and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada). 

2. Unit Economics: Commercial sales volumes remain low. For example, during FY2025, over half of Agility's total revenue was generated by just 5 robots purchased by a single strategic investor, most likely Amazon.
- Operating Hours: Humanoid units have logged a combined total of over 65,000 commercial operating hours across customer facilities. That’s about 12 years of experience for 1 unit.
- Pricing & Revenue Models: Agility offers both capital sales and a Robotics-as-a-Service (RaaS) subscription model:
Purchase: ~$100,000 to $250,000 per unit.  
RaaS Subscription Structure: Upfront Deployment & Onboarding: ~$25,000   Recurring Subscription: ~$8,000 – $10,000 per month (includes software licensing and maintenance).   5-Year Revenue per Unit: Agility projects that a single robot yields approximately $400,000 in revenue over a 5-year operational lifecycle.

Utility: Digit's deployments focus on repetitive, non-prehensile material handling in warehouse and manufacturing environments (that’s moving objects without fully grasping or closing fine fingers around them). Specific tasks Digit v4 is reported to perform include
- picking up empty or loaded plastic totes, weighing between 25 and 35 lbs, from automation systems and transferring them to conveyors or staging carts. That load capacity increases to 50 lbs for the upcoming Digit v5 model.
- sorting, moving, and stacking industrial parts and totes between workstations.
- Navigating narrow warehouse aisles, ramps, and stairs to transport heavy items across facilities.
Logistics:
- Duty Cycle: ~16 to 18 hours of active work per 24-hour day. Digit v4 runs for approximately 2 hours per charge and requires autonomous docking to recharge for roughly 30 minutes with an option for autonomous battery-swapping to return to work quickly. The Run-to-Charge Ratio is ~4:1. Scheduled Service per month: –25 to 27 hours. Unanticipated Downtime per month: ~35 to 38 hours

A ‘back of the envelope’ calculation of RaaS variable costs adds up to ~455 productive hours in a 30 day month yielding ~57 8-hour shifts at ~$17.58-21.98/hr. So, ~2x the productivity of a human line worker at less cost.

Future demand: GXO Logistics is expanding its deployment of Agility’s Digit humanoid robot to two additional U.S. warehouses in Statesville, North Carolina and Lebanon, Tennessee in addition to Flowery Branch, Georgia. Digit will handle repetitive material-handling work supporting e-commerce fulfillment at both sites, starting in early 2027. This means that at least that one customer is satisfied with the product and ordered more.
In the past few months, Agility has launched Digit v5, announced a Pittsburgh expansion and added a new customer, farm equipment maker AGCO, to pilot Digit v5. Agility reported over $300M in committed multi-year backlog and commercial orders. However, the vast majority of these multi-unit commercial deliveries are scheduled to begin scaling revenue recognition in 2027 as volume production ramps at its RoboFab facility in Salem, Oregon.

All this as Agility executed it’s SPAC deal last week on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol AGLT. Generating roughly $465M in new capital, it marks the first publicly traded pure-play humanoid robotics company in the U.S.
- Final pre-money valuation of $2.5B.
- PIPE (private investment in public equity) financing included $201 million at $10.00 per share.
- Upon closing, existing Agility stockholders own approximately 72.7%, SPAC public shareholders 14.9%, the SPAC Sponsor 5.1%, and PIPE investors 7.3%. 
- The equity closed last week at $9.90/share.

Financial Disclosures:
- 2025 Revenue: $1.8 million.
- A 2025 $140 million operating loss, underscoring the high capital intensity and burn rate involved in scaling commercial humanoid robots prior to mass adoption.
Use of Funds:
~$620M is designated to scale manufacturing of its flagship humanoid robot, Digit v5, at its Oregon RoboFab facility.
- Funding customer deployments (including logistics partners such as GXO) and expanding the Agility Arc software platform.

While this is not a particularly compelling case for buying the SPAC, it does provide meaningful market data on humanoid utility in terms of some customers willing to pay for Digit v5 to perform limited repetitive tasks at an apparently competitive price of ~$17.58-21.98/hr. Maybe humanoids have utility?

@elonmusk

With the help of Grok:  correct course!  Space, surebut not near term.

Yes, he has real reasons to be concerned about the concentration in Texas — at least for new AI/data-center and large-scale infrastructure projects.​
Newsweek
Texas just had a historic political shift. In the November 3, 2026 midterms, Democrats swept statewide offices for the first time in decades. Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott for governor, and James Talarico won the U.S. Senate seat. Democrats also flipped the Texas House. Hinojosa campaigned explicitly on an “immediate moratorium” (a ban) on new data-center approvals until the legislature passes “real protections” for Texans on water use, electricity costs, local control, and incentives. She takes office in January 2027. Texas holds a large share of planned U.S. data-center capacity (estimates around a quarter), so this directly hits the sector that powered much of the recent AI-driven growth.​
Datacenterdynamics
Musk’s exposure in Texas
Musk has heavily concentrated there:
Tesla’s Gigafactory Texas
SpaceX’s Starbase
The planned Terafab semiconductor complex in Grimes County (SpaceX/Tesla, with an initial ~$16.8 billion investment, potentially much larger)
Ongoing exploration of large-scale data centers and related AI infrastructure
He spent hundreds of millions supporting Republicans in the midterms (including significant sums in Texas). After the results, he posted that “data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” Tesla and SpaceX shares both dropped sharply in the Thursday sell-off tied to these regulatory fears.
Existing manufacturing and launch operations are harder to unwind and face less immediate threat than new data-center permits. But the political climate that made Texas the easiest, fastest place to build large projects has changed.
Oklahoma and Wyoming as alternatives
Both remain far more consistently pro-business and Republican-controlled right now:
Oklahoma has a growing data-center pipeline, relatively low industrial power costs, active projects (including Google), and fewer statewide barriers so far. It has some ratepayer-protection rules but nothing like a moratorium.
Wyoming is even more attractive on paper for pure infrastructure: abundant cheap energy (coal and wind), open land, low taxes, low population density, high per-capita data-center activity, and active large projects from companies like Meta and others. It has stayed solidly red.

**Low — realistically under 10%, and probably closer to single digits in the current lame-duck session.**

The strategy Mike Lee outlined (put the bill on the floor, force a pure talking filibuster, then vote by simple majority once opponents stop speaking, and keep going until it passes) is a known idea he and others pushed for much of 2026. It has not worked so far.[](<https://t.co/5bGKZJbilU>)

Key reasons the odds stay low:

- **It already failed to clear the 60-vote bar repeatedly.** Cloture votes and related procedural moves topped out around 52–53 votes. Several Republicans (Collins, Murkowski, McConnell, Tillis at various points) opposed key amendments or maneuvers. Senate leadership under Thune has consistently said the votes for either 60 or a sustained rules fight/talking filibuster were not there.[](<https://t.co/Pt8B0sLrNJ>)

- **Talking filibuster is hard to force in practice.** It requires the majority to fully control the floor, stay unified for days or weeks of continuous debate, and overcome the modern Senate’s preference for cloture. Leadership and many rank-and-file Republicans have been reluctant because of the disruption, the precedent, and the risk it fails anyway. Earlier attempts and discussions did not produce passage.[](<https://t.co/MzziPCR6kG>)

- **Election results make it even less likely.** Democrats flipped the Senate (projected 54+ seats once Alaska and Mississippi finish). The current Republican 53–47 majority only lasts until January 3, 2027. After a midterm loss, many Republicans have less incentive to grind the chamber to a halt on a high-profile bill that Democrats will control next year. Lame-duck priorities usually shift toward must-pass items or winding down, not a multi-week filibuster fight.[](<https://t.co/9z269MVuuV>)

Betting markets earlier in 2026 already priced the bill’s chances in the low single digits to low teens. Nothing in the post-election environment improves those odds; if anything, it worsens them. A successful pure exhaustion-to-simple-majority outcome remains theoretically possible if Republicans suddenly achieve perfect unity and leadership commits fully, but the track record and incentives point against it.

text:
ROUND XVII
THE DAMNATION OF A DOCTRINE AND OF ALL WHO ENFORCE IT
FROM ITS OWN TEXTS AND THE RECORDS OF NATIONS, MEDINA TO THIS YEAR

From 627 to 2026, by its own texts and by the records of the United Nations, of this Republic and of its allies, the doctrine of death for the apostate and the blasphemer, of the poll tax and the humbled, of the woman as half and the child as bride, of the captive as property, and of war upon those who will not submit, stands damned. Every state, court, council, guard corps and movement that enforces it stands condemned.

There is no reprieve.

Kept by a citizen of the United States, under the First Amendment. Every source is in the Record, on request.

Here, "It" is that doctrine, and every state, court, council, guard corps and movement that enforces it, and every hand that takes up its sword. Its first dead are its own: the Muslims who would not submit.

I. THE TEXTS

Each text verbatim, in Arabic and English.

The apostate. Heretics were brought to Ali, and he burned them. Ibn Abbas said: I would not have burned them, for the Messenger of God forbade it: "Do not punish with God's punishment." I would have killed them, for the Messenger of God said:
من بدل دينه فاقتلوه
"Whoever changes his religion, kill him." (Sahih al-Bukhari 6922)

The People of the Book.
قاتلوا الذين لا يؤمنون بالله ولا باليوم الآخر ولا يحرمون ما حرم الله ورسوله ولا يدينون دين الحق من الذين أوتوا الكتاب حتى يعطوا الجزية عن يد وهم صاغرون
"Fight those who do not believe in God or in the Last Day, who do not forbid what God and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not hold the religion of truth, among those given the Book, until they give the jizya out of hand, and they are humbled." (Quran 9:29)

Arabia. Umar heard the Messenger of God say:
لأخرجن اليهود والنصارى من جزيرة العرب حتى لا أدع إلا مسلما
"I will surely drive the Jews and the Christians out of the peninsula of the Arabs, until I leave none but Muslim." (Sahih Muslim 1767)

The Jew and the Christian. The Messenger of God said:
لا تبدءوا اليهود ولا النصارى بالسلام فإذا لقيتم أحدهم في طريق فاضطروه إلى أضيقه
"Do not be the first to greet the Jews or the Christians. When you meet one of them on a road, force him to its narrowest part." (Sahih Muslim 2167)

The woman. On a debt:
واستشهدوا شهيدين من رجالكم فإن لم يكونا رجلين فرجل وامرأتان ممن ترضون من الشهداء أن تضل إحداهما فتذكر إحداهما الأخرى
"And call two witnesses from your men; and if they are not two men, then a man and two women, of those you accept as witnesses, so that if one of the two strays, the one reminds the other." (Quran 2:282)
On the wife:
الرجال قوامون على النساء بما فضل الله بعضهم على بعض وبما أنفقوا من أموالهم فالصالحات قانتات حافظات للغيب بما حفظ الله واللاتي تخافون نشوزهن فعظوهن واهجروهن في المضاجع واضربوهن فإن أطعنكم فلا تبغوا عليهن سبيلا إن الله كان عليا كبيرا
"Men are in charge of women, by what God has favored some of them over others, and by what they spend of their wealth. So the righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in the unseen what God has guarded. And those whose defiance you fear: admonish them, and forsake them in the beds, and strike them. If they obey you, seek no way against them. God is ever High, Great." (Quran 4:34)

The child bride. From Aisha:
أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم تزوجها وهي بنت ست سنين وأدخلت عليه وهي بنت تسع ومكثت عنده تسعا
"That the Prophet married her when she was six years old and he consummated his marriage when she was nine years old, and then she remained with him for nine years." (Sahih al-Bukhari 5133)

The captive.
والذين هم لفروجهم حافظون إلا على أزواجهم أو ما ملكت أيمانهم فإنهم غير ملومين
"And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands own, for then they are not blamed." (Quran 23:5–6)
والمحصنات من النساء إلا ما ملكت أيمانكم
"And [forbidden to you are] the married among women, except what your right hands own." (Quran 4:24)

War on God.
إنما جزاء الذين يحاربون الله ورسوله ويسعون في الأرض فسادا أن يقتلوا أو يصلبوا أو تقطع أيديهم وأرجلهم من خلاف أو ينفوا من الأرض ذلك لهم خزي في الدنيا ولهم في الآخرة عذاب عظيم
"The recompense of those who wage war on God and His Messenger, and strive in the land for corruption, is only that they be killed, or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off from opposite sides, or be banished from the land. That is their disgrace in this world, and in the Hereafter theirs is a great punishment." (Quran 5:33)
إذ يوحي ربك إلى الملائكة أني معكم فثبتوا الذين آمنوا سألقي في قلوب الذين كفروا الرعب فاضربوا فوق الأعناق واضربوا منهم كل بنان
"When your Lord inspired the angels: I am with you, so make firm those who believed. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike above the necks, and strike from them every fingertip." (Quran 8:12)

Allegiance and concealment.
يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تتخذوا اليهود والنصارى أولياء بعضهم أولياء بعض ومن يتولهم منكم فإنه منهم إن الله لا يهدي القوم الظالمين
"O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. Whoever of you takes them as allies is one of them. God does not guide the wrongdoing people." (Quran 5:51)
لا يتخذ المؤمنون الكافرين أولياء من دون المؤمنين ومن يفعل ذلك فليس من الله في شيء إلا أن تتقوا منهم تقاة ويحذركم الله نفسه وإلى الله المصير
"Let not the believers take the unbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Whoever does that has nothing of God, unless you guard yourselves against them with a guarding. And God warns you of Himself, and to God is the return." (Quran 3:28)
It is mentioned from Abu al-Darda:
إنا لنكشر في وجوه أقوام وإن قلوبنا لتلعنهم
"We grin in the faces of some peoples, and our hearts curse them." (Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Manners)

The raised grave. Ali sent Abu al-Hayyaj on the errand the Messenger of God gave him:
أن لا تدع تمثالا إلا طمسته ولا قبرا مشرفا إلا سويته
"That you leave no image without effacing it, and no raised grave without levelling it." (Sahih Muslim 969)

The command. Ibn Umar: the Messenger of God said:
أمرت أن أقاتل الناس حتى يشهدوا أن لا إله إلا الله وأن محمدا رسول الله ويقيموا الصلاة ويؤتوا الزكاة فإذا فعلوا ذلك عصموا مني دماءهم وأموالهم إلا بحق الإسلام وحسابهم على الله
"I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and establish the prayer, and give the zakat. If they do that, they have protected their blood and their wealth from me, except by the right of Islam, and their reckoning is with God." (Sahih al-Bukhari 25)

II. FROM MEDINA TO CLERMONT, 627 TO 1095

It has beheaded six to nine hundred men of the Banu Qurayza in trenches dug in the market of Medina, 627, and enslaved their women and children.

It has driven the Jews and Christians out of the Hejaz, under Umar, to Tayma and Jericho.

It has seized the cathedral of St John the Baptist at Damascus, long shared, and made it al-Walid's great mosque, 705.

It has broken Persia at Qadisiyyah and Nahavand, taken Egypt, and laid Carthage waste, 636 to 698.

It has taken from Nubia, which beat it back at Dongola in 652, a treaty of 360 slaves a year, sent north for centuries.

It has besieged Constantinople twice, 674 to 678 and 717 to 718. Twice the city held.

It has sacked St Peter's and St Paul Outside the Walls, at Rome in 846. The Pope walled the Vatican hill.

It has ordered the Holy Sepulchre destroyed at Jerusalem in 1009, with churches and synagogues across Egypt, Palestine and Syria.

It has burned the temples of Mathura, 1018, on an order its own chronicler records: all of them "burnt with naphtha and fire, and levelled to the ground." It has sacked Somnath and its temple, 1026.

It has broken Byzantium at Manzikert, 1071, and taken most of Anatolia. In November 1095, at Clermont, the Crusade was called.

From the trenches of Medina to Clermont: 468 years.

III. FROM CLERMONT, 1095 TO 1700

It has given the Jews and Christians of Ifriqiya and Spain conversion, exile or death, from 1151.

It has raised Delhi's first great mosque in the 1190s from the carved columns of twenty-seven Hindu and Jain temples. Its own inscription says so.

It has put to the sword, before Delhi in December 1398, the Hindu prisoners of Timur's march: a hundred thousand, by his own chronicler's count.

It has taken Constantinople, 1453, the city that held twice, and made Hagia Sophia a mosque. In 2020 Turkey made it a mosque again, and the Chora church after it.

It has beheaded 813 men at Otranto, 14 August 1480, who would not renounce their faith. The Church made them saints in 2013.

It has taken boys from Christian households, converted them, and made them Janissaries, for three centuries.

It has waged jihad on Christian Ethiopia, 1529 to 1543, burning churches and seizing three-quarters of the land, until Portuguese musketeers turned it back.

It has carried some two million captives out of Poland-Lithuania and Russia in the Crimean raids, 1500 to 1700.

It has carried off more than 400 Icelanders in 1627 and more than 100 from Baltimore in Ireland in 1631, mostly women and children, to sell.

It has driven more than ten million Africans across the Sahara, the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean into the slave markets of its lands, 650 to 1900.

It has ordered the governors of every province to demolish the schools and temples of the unbelievers, April 1669, in its own chronicler's words. It has razed the temple of Vishwanath at Kashi that year and Keshav Rai's at Mathura the next, and buried the idols under the steps of a mosque at Agra, to be trodden on.

It has executed Guru Tegh Bahadur, ninth Guru of the Sikhs, at Delhi in November 1675, on Aurangzeb's order, for opposing forced conversions. In 1679 it restored the jizya.

From Clermont to the Tripoli envoy in London: 691 years.

IV. THE ACCOUNT OF THIS REPUBLIC

It has made war on this Republic since its first years. Asked in London, March 1786, by what right Tripoli made war on nations that had done it no injury, its envoy told Adams and Jefferson "it was founded on the Laws of their Prophet," "that it was written in their Koran, that all nations who should not have acknowledged their authority were sinners," "that it was their right and duty to make war upon them wherever they could be found," "and that every Musselman who should be slain in battle was sure to go to Paradise."

It has held 89 American sailors for ransom at Algiers, some for eleven years, and taken from us a yearly tribute of about 16 percent of our appropriated budget, 1795 to 1796.

It has answered our peace with demands. In 1797 our Senate ratified a treaty declaring this Republic bore "no character of enmity against the laws, religion or tranquility of Musselmen." In 1801 Tripoli answered "with demands unfounded either in right or in compact." We answered with the Navy.

It has held 52 Americans hostage at our embassy in Tehran for 444 days, 1979 to 1981, and eight of ours died trying to bring them home. It has killed seventeen sailors on the USS Cole at Aden, 2000, and four Americans at Benghazi, 2012, Ambassador Stevens among them.

It has decreed, 23 February 1998, in what its authors called a fatwa, "that every Muslim should try his utmost to kill any American, military or civilian, anywhere in the world." In August 1998 it bombed our embassies in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam: 224 killed, 12 of them Americans. On 11 September 2001 it killed more than 2,600 at the World Trade Center, 125 at the Pentagon and 256 on the four planes.

It has killed seventeen of ours at our embassy in Beirut and 241 servicemen at the Marine barracks, 1983, and nineteen airmen at Khobar Towers, 1996. It keeps a Guard whose constitutional charge is "the ideological mission of jihad in God's way," named by us a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 2019. The regime it guards is "responsible for the deaths of at least 603 American service members in Iraq since 2003." A federal court has held Iran and its Guard liable for 11 September. This year's war with Iran: 21 of ours dead, 865 wounded. In August its army priced each of our soldiers at $30,000, killed or captured, double if a woman does it; its Guard's media, the President's son at $10 million.

It has put a $500,000 price on the life of Masih Alinejad, a journalist in New York, 2022. The hired man bought an AK-47 and stalked her home. Convicted, March 2025; twenty-five years each.

It has stabbed Salman Rushdie on stage at Chautauqua, New York, 2022. The man "attempted to carry out a fatwa," said the Director of the FBI: Khomeini's, endorsed by Hezbollah. Twenty-five years from New York; a federal terrorism conviction, 29 July 2026.

It has murdered about 1,200 on 7 October 2023, more than forty of them Americans, and taken 251 hostage, twelve of them American. The killers' covenant names Hamas a wing of the Muslim Brotherhood and quotes the hadith of the stones and trees: "there is a Jew behind me, come and kill him."

Detroit, 2017: the first prosecution under our federal ban on female genital mutilation, a doctor charged with cutting girls of seven. In 2018 a federal judge held the law beyond Congress's power and threw out the charges against members of a Muslim sect; Congress rewrote it in 2021 and doubled the maximum to ten years.

From Tripoli to New Orleans, it has killed at least 5,400 of ours. Nearly 3,000 more fell in Iraq to hands never recorded.

V. THE BROTHERHOOD, IN ITS OWN WORDS AND IN GOVERNMENTS' FINDINGS

It has raised the Muslim Brotherhood, founded by Hassan al-Banna at Ismailia, 1928. Its motto ends: "Jihad is our way. Dying in the way of Allah is our highest hope." Its aim, as the British government records it: Muslim societies' "eventual political unification in a Caliphate under sharia law."

It has taught, through Sayyid Qutb in Milestones, 1964, that the goal is "the establishing of the dominion of God on earth," and that preaching must be joined by jihad.

It has named its work in America, in the Brotherhood's 1991 memorandum entered in evidence at the federal Holy Land Foundation trial, "a kind of grand Jihad in eliminating and destroying the Western civilization from within."

It has promised, through Yusuf al-Qaradawi, the Brotherhood's jurist, that "Islam will return to Europe as a conqueror and victor," this time by preaching and ideology.

It countenances violence, "including, from time to time, terrorism - where gradualism is ineffective," the British government found in December 2015; it "deliberately, wittingly and openly incubated and sustained" Hamas. In Britain its membership "remained (and still remains) a secret."

It builds from below in France, through associations and town halls: "une menace pour la cohésion nationale," the French government reported in May 2025, with 139 places of worship, 280 associations and 21 private schools tied to the movement.

It funds Hamas. On 13 January 2026 we named the Lebanese Brotherhood a Foreign Terrorist Organization and designated the Egyptian and Jordanian branches "for providing material support to Hamas." On 23 July a senior UK-based Egyptian Brotherhood official, three others and three entities were designated for moving funds to Hamas through "charitable facades and underground networks."

VI. ITS RULINGS AND ITS WARS, 1971 TO NOW

It has raised Al-Badr, the Islamist militia that rode beside Pakistan's army in 1971 and murdered the intellectuals of Bangladesh two days before the surrender. As the army struck, our consul general in Dacca cabled Washington under the subject "Selective Genocide," the Hindus among the marked. Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal convicted Al-Badr's chiefs, and they hanged.

It has imposed its law on Sudan, 1983, and the war that followed in the south took about two million lives by 2005. In 1992 its governors declared jihad on the Nuba, sealed by a fatwa at El Obeid that branded even the Muslims among them apostates.

It has put thousands of prisoners to death in secret, Iran, summer 1988, on Khomeini's order: the Mojahedin as moharebs, those who war on God, the leftists as apostates. It hides their graves still.

It has sentenced Salman Rushdie to death, with those who published his book, and keeps the sentence: Khomeini's decree, Tehran, 14 February 1989. The 15 Khordad Foundation, "affiliated with the Supreme Leader," set a price on him, raised in 2012 to $3.3 million. Asked in 2017 whether the decree stood, Khamenei answered: "The decree is as Imam Khomeini issued." In 2019 his office called it "solid and irrevocable."

It has driven the Hindus from the Kashmir valley: from 1990, under the guns of the jihadist insurgency, more than sixty thousand families fled.

It has handed out the Islamic State's pamphlet in Mosul, December 2014, after Friday sunset prayers: Questions and Answers on Taking Captives and Slaves. Unbelieving women may be bought, sold or given as gifts, "for they are merely property"; intercourse is permitted with a slave girl who has not reached puberty. It cites the Quran's "what their right hands own."

It has ruled, from Qom, 29 June 2025, through Grand Ayatollah Naser Makarem Shirazi, that any person or regime threatening the Leader or a marja is a "mohareb," one who wages war on God. Iran's law carries the verse's penalties: death, crucifixion, amputation, exile.

It has ruled the cut part of its law. Indonesia, 2008: the Ulema Council ruled female circumcision part of Sharia; about half of Indonesia's girls aged eleven and under have been cut. Malaysia, 2009: the National Fatwa Council ruled it obligatory for Muslim women unless harmful.

VII. IN FORCE NOW

It hangs the apostate. Twenty-two countries make apostasy a crime; not one in Europe or the Americas. Khartoum, 18 January 1985: it hanged Mahmoud Mohamed Taha, a Muslim theologian of seventy-six, for opposing Sharia law.

It writes stoning into law. Brunei, April 2019: stoning for adultery and sodomy, death for apostasy and for contempt of the Prophet, took effect. Held under a royal moratorium. Kept on the books.

It kills the blasphemer. Eight countries allow death for blasphemy. Islamabad, 2011: Governor Salmaan Taseer, a Muslim, shot dead by his own bodyguard for opposing the blasphemy law; thousands mourned the killer when he hanged. Jaranwala, 2023: a mob of hundreds damaged dozens of churches and homes after two Christians were accused of desecrating the Quran. Paris, 2015: twelve killed at Charlie Hebdo. Conflans-Sainte-Honorine, 2020: Samuel Paty beheaded outside his school for showing the cartoons in a class on free expression.

It takes the child bride. Sikh, Hindu and Christian girls taken, converted and married, "often with authorities failing to intervene." In 2026 Pakistan's Federal Constitutional Court upheld the forced marriage of a Christian girl abducted at thirteen.

It halves the woman. Iran: "The diya (blood-money) for murdering a woman is half that of a man," and offenses punishable by diya are proved by one man and two women. Pakistan: a written financial obligation is attested "by two men, or one man and two women." Its Zina Ordinance of 1979 punished rape with stoning or a hundred lashes on "at least four Muslim adult male witnesses," until rape was moved into the Penal Code in 2006.

It kills women in custody and bars girls from school. Tehran: Mahsa Amini, 22, arrested over her hijab, dead in the morality police's custody; "physical violence in custody led to Ms. Amini's unlawful death." Kabul: girls barred from secondary school, women from universities since 20 December 2022, and under the 2024 vice-and-virtue law "even the sound of a female voice" outside the home a moral violation.

It offers the Christian conversion, the jizya, flight or the sword. Mosul, July 2014: so it ordered, and hundreds of families fled.

It enslaves. Slavery was abolished in Saudi Arabia only in 1962; in Mauritania in 1981, and made a crime there only in 2007. Nouakchott, 2012: the abolitionist Biram Dah Abeid burned pages of a Maliki law text that asserts slavery is embraced by the faith, and was arrested. Sinjar, 2014: "clear and convincing evidence that genocide was committed by ISIL against the Yazidi as a religious group," whose women it declared enslavable as spoils of war.

Under its rule the dancing boys are kept still. Afghanistan: bacha bazi, boys kept and abused by powerful men. Our own inspector general found Afghan officials "complicit, especially in the sexual exploitation and recruitment of children," and our Defense Department kept funding units implicated in gross violations. Banned by the republic in 2018 and by the Taliban, it goes on: Taliban members among the perpetrators, and "a pattern of sexual slavery" under their rule.

It razes the holy places. Bamiyan, 2001: the Buddhas dynamited. Timbuktu, 2012: nine saints' mausoleums and the door of the Sidi Yahia mosque taken to with pickaxes, to eradicate what "can lead to idolatry"; a war-crimes conviction at the International Criminal Court. Egypt, 14 August 2013: at least 42 churches attacked, 37 burned or damaged, police and army absent. Mosul and Nineveh, 2014 to 2015: the shrine of Jonah blown up; the museum's statues smashed as idols; Nimrud bulldozed; Hatra, "cultural cleansing." Palmyra, 2015: the Temples of Bel and Baalshamin blown up, "a new war crime." By men sworn to or claimed by the Islamic State: Saint-Étienne-du-Rouvray, 26 July 2016, Father Jacques Hamel, 85, forced to his knees at the altar during Mass, his throat cut; Berlin, December 2016, twelve killed at the Christmas market; Cairo, December 2016, 29 killed in the church of Sts Peter and Paul; Tanta and Alexandria, Palm Sunday 2017, at least 45 killed at two churches; Sri Lanka, Easter Sunday 2019, three churches bombed at worship, more than 200 dead. Nice, October 2020: three killed inside the Notre-Dame basilica, one nearly beheaded.

It seats councils of its own in Britain. London, 2016: the Home Office found "evidence some sharia councils may be working in a discriminatory and unacceptable way, seeking to legitimise forced marriage." Its 2018 review: no one who gave evidence disputed that the councils discriminate against women. The Home Office declined to regulate them. Britain, from 2014: hundreds of schools went halal-only for every child; the Sikh Council protested it was served "without declaring it as such."

Rochdale and Oldham, 2008 to 2010. Girls in their early teens, raped, and driven to men who paid for them. Sentencing nine men in 2012, the judge found they had treated the girls "as though they were worthless and beyond all respect," and that one of the factors "was that they were not of your community or religion."

The United Nations seats on its Human Rights Council, through 2028, Pakistan, whose penal code prescribes death for blasphemy, elected by 178 votes. In April it nominated Iran over our lone objection, and on 11 November elected it, by 144 votes, to the committee that helps set its priorities on human rights and women's rights. text:
The White House says, "STAND. FIGHT. DEFEND THE REPUBLIC." Defending the republic also means a Republican Party that can win.

One week before Election Day, Alaska's senior U.S. senator, Lisa Murkowski (R), went on KTUU, Anchorage's NBC station, and endorsed the Democrat for governor, former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D) of Sitka. Her father, former Gov. and Sen. Frank Murkowski (R), endorsed him the same day with former Govs. Tony Knowles (D) and Bill Walker (I).

She passed over three Republicans: Bernadette Wilson (R), whom President Trump (R) endorsed; former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson (R); and former Attorney General Treg Taylor (R). The Republican Party of Alaska never endorsed any of them.

THE COUNT
In the Division of Elections' Nov. 10 report, Kreiss-Tomkins has 49.74% of first-choice votes. The three Republicans together have 49.97%. That does not mean Republicans would have won. Under Alaska's ranked-choice rules, votes move only to the next candidate a voter ranked. About a third of Taylor's ballots and more than a third of Bronson's ranked no one else, so they stopped counting. A preview of the final round puts Kreiss-Tomkins at about 55.6%.

In the Senate race, Mary Peltola (D) leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) by 4,250 votes. Neither race is certified yet.

HOW IT HAPPENED
Twelve Republicans ran for governor in the August top-four primary, where every candidate runs on one ballot and the top four advance. The best of them got 10%. The Democrats had two. Tom Begich (D) finished second, dropped out and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins. No Republican stepped aside.

MURKOWSKI'S PATTERN
- 2010: Lost the GOP primary to Joe Miller (R), won as a write-in anyway.
- 2021: Censured by the state party for voting to convict Trump.
- 2022: Ranked Peltola (D) first for the U.S. House, then beat party-endorsed Kelly Tshibaka (R).
- 2024: Endorsed Peltola over Nick Begich (R).
- 2026: Backed Sullivan (R) over Peltola for Senate, but the Democrat for governor.

HER VOTES, FROM SENATE ROLL CALLS
- 2017: One of three Republicans who killed the Obamacare "skinny repeal," 49-51.
- 2018: The only Republican to vote no on ending debate over Brett Kavanaugh.
- 2021: One of seven Republicans who voted to convict Trump, 57-43.
- 2022: Voted for Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, the gun bill and the Respect for Marriage Act. She voted NO on the Inflation Reduction Act, with every Republican.
- 2025: Voted no on Pete Hegseth, confirmed only by the vice president's tie-break, and on Kash Patel. Voted yes on Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
- 2025–26: Repeatedly voted to end Trump's tariff emergencies and for war powers limits on Venezuela and Iran.

FOLLOW THE MONEY
FEC filings show the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC tied to Mitch McConnell (R), spent $6.1 million against Tshibaka in 2022. A pro-Murkowski super PAC raised $5.1 million. Murkowski's own leadership PAC gave $67,000 to McConnell's super PAC.

Alaska Public Offices Commission filings show Unite America has put more than $14.4 million into Alaska since 2020, nearly all of it to create and defend this voting system. The 2026 repeal was funded almost entirely by one Wisconsin committee, Aurora Action Network, which got $1.5 million from Elon Musk. The repeal is failing by almost 12,000 votes, wider than its 743-vote loss in 2024.

THE SAME CRACKS, NATIONWIDE
Former Republican governors in Kansas and South Carolina backed Democrats for Senate, and the Democrats won. In Texas, Ken Paxton (R) beat Sen. John Cornyn (R) in the primary, then lost to James Talarico (D), 55.1% to 43%. NBC News reported Democrats flipped five governorships in states Trump carried in 2024.

WHAT THE GOP MUST FIX
Settle the field before the ballot does it for you. Teach your voters to rank. Stop spending primaries on revenge. Give voters a reason, not just a label. Murkowski's own seat is up in 2028 under the same rules.

The full article is here:

Microsoft ($MSFT) pledged to cover its own data-center power costs without government subsidies or shifting expenses onto other electricity customers, as opposition to AI infrastructure grows.

* Energy Commitment: Cloud operations President Noelle Walsh said Microsoft will "pay our own way" as it plans $117B in AI and cloud computing capacity this year, aiming to ensure communities benefit from development.
* Texas Project: Microsoft is partnering with Chevron ($CVX) and Engine No. 1 on Project Kilby, a large data-center and power development designed to generate electricity on-site in West Texas.
* Regulatory Delays: The project faces Texas' moratorium on new data-center approvals. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has signaled potentially tougher permitting restrictions after defeating Greg Abbott.
* Timeline & Benefits: Chevron still targets initial operations by 2028 and full operation by 2031, citing local jobs and stable tax revenue as community benefits.

text:
Per Grok: **No, there is no clear evidence that Memphis residents have faced higher electric or water bills specifically because of data centers.** Utility officials have repeatedly stated the opposite, and new rate structures are designed to make data centers pay more (or their full share) rather than shift costs to households.

### Electricity

- MLGW President and CEO Doug McGowen has stated unequivocally that “There have been no rates changed for residential, commercial or industrial class customers because of data centers in Memphis and Shelby County.” Data centers must pay upfront capacity charges (around $1.5 million per megawatt for large loads) to cover grid upgrades so residents do not.
- Recent residential electricity increases (a 12% hike approved in 2023 and phased in through early 2026, adding roughly $5/month for an average household) were tied to grid modernization and reliability improvements, not data-center demand.
- In August 2026, the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA, MLGW’s power supplier) created a separate higher rate class for data centers. Existing data centers face about a 10% rate increase phased over three years, plus capacity commitment charges for large new loads. The explicit goal is to protect residential and other customers from subsidizing data-center power demand.

A July 2026 ThinkTennessee report found that Tennessee areas with data centers saw slightly higher average residential bill increases than the statewide average between 2023 and 2024 (roughly 1.6% vs. 1.3%, with residential customers in those areas seeing about 3.2%). This is a correlation across the state rather than direct proof of causation in Memphis, where pre-existing rate plans and the new protective structures apply.

### Water

- Facilities such as xAI’s Colossus have used substantial amounts of water (on the order of hundreds of thousands of gallons per day from the Memphis Sand Aquifer in recent periods), and plans for a large recycling/wastewater facility have faced delays. This has raised legitimate local concerns about aquifer stress, especially given the region’s sole reliance on that aquifer for drinking water.
- However, MLGW has approved (or proposed) higher rates specifically for data centers—around 30% for water—compared with lower increases for residential customers (around 12%). Officials have stated that the residential water and gas rate hikes (phased starting in 2027, adding roughly $2.50–$10/month for water and $6–$18/month for gas for average households by 2029) are driven by general infrastructure needs, aging systems, higher operating costs, and the exhaustion of reserves—not by data-center infrastructure. Leadership has emphasized that none of the residential increases will fund data-center projects.

Industrial users have historically paid lower per-gallon water rates than households, which has drawn criticism from groups like Protect Our Aquifer. Newer dedicated data-center rate classes and capacity rules aim to reverse any preferential treatment.

**Bottom line:** Rate increases have occurred in Memphis, and data centers create real resource-demand issues (especially water and peak power), but available evidence from MLGW, TVA, and related reporting does not show residents paying higher bills *because of* those facilities. Protective rate structures and laws are in place to prevent cost-shifting. Environmental and aquifer concerns remain separate from the question of residential bill impacts.

Industrial users have historically paid lower per-gallon water rates than households, which has drawn criticism from groups like Protect Our Aquifer. Newer dedicated data-center rate classes and capacity rules aim to reverse any preferential treatment.

**Bottom line:** Rate increases have occurred in Memphis, and data centers create real resource-demand issues (especially water and peak power), but available evidence from MLGW, TVA, and related reporting does not show residents paying higher bills *because of* those facilities. Protective rate structures and laws are in place to prevent cost-shifting. Environmental and aquifer concerns remain separate from the question of residential bill impacts.

text:
Texas Supreme Court Majority Now One Retirement Away From Democratic Control

After last week’s blue wave flipped the Texas governorship and four Supreme Court seats, the state’s highest civil court sits at a precarious 5-4 Republican edge. Justice Debra Lehrmann, the longest-serving member and a Republican appointed by Rick Perry in 2010, is openly weighing an early exit before her term ends in 2028. If she leaves before then, Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa gets to appoint the replacement and hand Democrats the majority for the first time in decades.

Lehrmann told Bloomberg she has not ruled out retiring early and must decide by early summer. She insisted politics will not factor into her choice and expressed faith that Hinojosa will pick a solid jurist. That faith is untested. Hinojosa just ended three decades of Republican governors, and the four new Democratic justices already elected this cycle mark the first Democratic presence on the court since the mid-1990s. An appointed fifth would lock in progressive control over the body that shapes Texas business law, property rights, school funding, and regulatory challenges.

Republicans have long used strategic retirements to let governors of their own party fill vacancies. Lehrmann now faces the reverse: complete her term and preserve the slim majority, or step aside and accelerate the shift. At 69, she could also finish the term and run again in 2028, though Texas’s age limit would force her off the bench midway through a new six-year term. The practical effect of any early departure is the same: one personal decision converts a narrow conservative hold into a Democratic majority on the court that decides the bulk of civil cases in the nation’s second-largest state.

The 2026 results already remade the bench. Incumbents including Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock and Justices James Sullivan, Kyle Hawkins, and Brett Busby lost. That leaves Lehrmann, John Devine, Jane Bland, Rebeca Huddle, and Evan Young as the remaining Republicans. Their majority is real but fragile, and it now depends on one justice choosing to stay.

text:
Key takeaways from the $CRWV (CoreWeave) Q3 2026 earnings call.

1. The oversupply fear got answered with pricing. New 4 to 5 year contracts now price at $20M to $25M per megawatt of capacity per year, and short-term deals go above $40M. Rental prices on older Nvidia chips (Ampere, Hopper) rose 30 to 50% QoQ, above their original contract rates. That is real evidence demand beats supply today. It says nothing about 2028, when the industry's new capacity lands. Intrator called 2028 sold out, then corrected himself in the same breath: only the slice they have offered so far has sold.

2. 2028 is being held back on purpose. That capacity has not been brought to market, and the stated reason is patience, waiting for better economics. Two readings: confidence that prices keep rising, or reluctance to lock in 2028 power and financing while credit markets are shaky. Both can be true. 

3. Returns after financing stay undisclosed. Asked for returns net of financing costs, the CFO gave payback periods instead: 6 to 18 months on short-term contracts, 1 to 2 years on long-term. Those paybacks are on hardware capex only, so data center build, power and interest sit outside them. No ceiling was given on how much capacity can sit in short-term deals either.

4. The quiet story is the paid-off fleet. About 130K GPUs come off contract in 2027 and about 170K in 2028. They were funded with DDTLs (delayed draw term loans, debt drawn as equipment arrives and repaid by the customer contract), so they come back debt-free. At current pricing, 2027 renewals add close to $4B of annualized revenue, nearly $10B including 2028, with zero new capex. More than $3B of the ~$9B in prepayments arriving over the next three months is already for re-contracted old gear. Caveat: the renewal figure sits outside the $133B backlog (signed revenue not yet earned) and assumes today's prices hold. It is an opportunity, not a contract.

5. The unsecured bond window is closed by choice. No new parent-level unsecured debt through 2027 at current yields. Funding shifts to contract-backed loans, prepayments (70% of deals this year carried one, some up to 100% of contract value), OEM financing and operating cash flow ($2B in Q3). The next DDTL launches in weeks, investment-grade, implied yield 7 to 7.5%, covering 90%+ of the capex. New parent-level capital needed through 2027: under $5B. Blended cost of debt is 7.9%, down 250bps YoY.

6. Diversification gets shown in customer counts, not dollars. 10% of the Fortune 500 are customers, more than half of 2026's new customers sit outside AI and tech, 10% of backlog is financial services, and 70% of new cloud customers came in through Forge (their AI developer toolkit). What the Q3 backlog growth was made of, and how fast the mix shifts away from frontier labs building their own compute: no breakdown. The closest dollar figure is 75%+ of committed 2027 capex tied to investment-grade and enterprise customers, a bucket that can include hyperscalers.

7. Regulatory exposure is described. They expect no impact from the post-election regulatory shift. In Texas, the overwhelming majority of their power is either online or permitted and under construction. No megawatt figure for Texas. The hedge is international: 1.3 GW of 4.6 GW contracted power is now outside the U.S., with new entries in India and Indonesia.

Bottom line: The operations are inflecting. Revenue +168% to $3.66B, 2026 guide raised to $13.0B to $13.3B, exit ARR (annualized run-rate revenue) of $20B to $21B, margins ahead of plan. Bullish for both $NBIS and $IREN.

Dr. Strangelove Now Speaks German. Paris Is Terrified.

A deterrent only works if the other side knows the rules, and France has just admitted to the Financial Times that Europe's newest one doesn't have any.

On the morning Europe layed its wreaths for the last great war it sleepwalked into, six people close to the talks between Paris and Berlin let the Financial Times know, in the careful language of officials who understand exactly what they are admitting, that the next one could begin with a German missile and a Russian officer who has a few minutes to guess what it means. One French official warned that Europe could "get to the nuclear threshold without realizing," which is a sentence that deserves to be carved over the door of every chancellery on the continent. Armistice Day, of all days.

Stanley Kubrick filmed Dr. Strangelove in 1964 and called it a comedy. The whole plot turns on a deterrent that fails because nobody bothered to tell the other side how it works, while Dr. Strangelove himself, the German scientist advising the President in the War Room, explains the logic of it all after the bombers have already left. 62 years later the script has been picked up in Europe and recast with a French president who fancies himself as le petit roi and a German chancellor who arrived via the BlackRock boardroom, and this time nobody is laughing. Least of all the French.

Because what Paris is asking for, once you strip away the diplomatic upholstery, is that Berlin's doctrine for "deep precision strikes" be tied to French nuclear strategy before the hardware shows up, and the reason offered by one source is that France has a nuclear "grammar and vocabulary" that Germany lacks. Translation: the only capital in the EU with its finger on a real button has read the German shopping list and reached for the defibrillator.
And the list is something to behold. 

Berlin has pledged €780 billion for defence through 2030, with roughly €12 billion going to a long-range arsenal that includes nearly €3.4 billion of American Tomahawks on mobile Typhon launchers and a classified missile project with the British that could be in service by 2034. The ranges run from 500 km to beyond 2,000, Berlin to Moscow is about 1,600, and nobody in the Russian General Staff needs that arithmetic explained to them.
The cast is as revealing as the catalogue. 

Merz has promised "the strongest conventional army in Europe," Pistorius has handed the Bundeswehr the first (suicidal) military strategy in its history with Russia written in as the main threat and 2039 (just in time for the Centennial!) as the deadline and the general chosen to run the whole machine from February is Christian Freuding, the officer who spent the war coordinating Germany's military aid to Ukraine. So here is a question from the cheap seats, Herr Merz. You have the range, the Ill gotten money stolen from Germans without a mandate for world war, the general and the deadline…. and by your closest ally's own account you do not have one published line explaining when you would fire, since no joint doctrine exists. What exactly is Moscow supposed to assume?

99 Luftballons, remixed
We have been in this cinema before. In November 1983 the Pershing IIs were arriving in West Germany with a flight time to Soviet command centres measured in minutes, a NATO exercise called Able Archer had convinced part of the Soviet leadership that the real thing might be hiding inside it, and a German pop song about a handful of balloons mistaken for an attack was climbing the charts across the West. The ground launched cruise missile parked in Europe in those years was an early Tomahawk with a nuclear warhead, Germany is now buying Tomahawks and Putin drew the Pershing comparison himself back in 2024. It took the INF Treaty to get the continent out of that trap and it took Washington walking out of the treaty in 2019 to put it back in. Brilliantly stupid and suicidal. 

Continue reading on our substack👇🏻

🇵🇱|The stage was set on November 11, 2026, in #Warsaw. The script was written by the usual authors: a "coup" in the Constitutional Court, a president standing with the "people," and a crowd presented as undeniable proof that the nation demands liberation from #Brussels.

But the #Polish street was not a spontaneous uprising. Instead, it was a carefully managed pressure valve, and the numbers behind the performance tell a far more controlled story.

🎭 **The Crowd: A Number That Tells Two Stories**

The official estimate from the Warsaw Safety Center put the Independence March at around 250,000 people, already a record for recent years. However, the organizers immediately inflated the figure, claiming between half a million and a million participants.

The claim that turnout was "three times the usual" was not an independent observation. Instead, it was the organizers' own estimate, based on the number of chartered buses. Meanwhile, the police and the city's own calculations suggested a lower figure, with one analysis placing the crowd between 120,000 and 160,000.

This is the first layer of the theater: a real and significant crowd is inflated into a mythic, unstoppable force to create the illusion of an overwhelming popular mandate.

⚖️ **The "Coup" Script: A Crisis Made for the Cameras**

The pretext was the Constitutional Tribunal crisis. On the night of October 30-31, 2026, the pro-EU government of Donald Tusk deployed police to the court, suspended its leadership, and installed loyalist judges through a side door.

The government described the move as "restoring the rule of law." However, the right-wing opposition, led by Jarosław Kaczyński, called it a "police state" and a "coup d'état."

President Karol Nawrocki, a PiS ally, dramatically turned his plane around mid-flight while travelling to Senegal. He then rushed to the court, physically forced his way through police lines, and declared that the constitutional order had been "violated."

This was not a spontaneous defence of democracy. Rather, it was a confrontation between two factions of the same political class, with both sides using the court as a prop to mobilize their respective political bases.

📊 **The Real POLEXIT: A Minority Project**

The most revealing fact is the one that celebratory videos will never show. Despite the massive crowd and the talk of "FREXIT" and "POLEXIT," actual public support for leaving the European Union remains a minority position.

Polls from late 2026 show that support for POLEXIT has doubled to around 20%. Although this represents a significant shift, it still amounts to only one in five Poles. Conversely, more than 70% of Poles want to remain in the EU. Furthermore, even when presented with various scenarios that might trigger an exit, the number of committed supporters rarely crosses 50%.

The march was not the voice of an entire nation demanding liberation. Instead, it was a show of force by a radicalized minority, comprising the electorates of PiS, Konfederacja and the far right, amplified by a media ecosystem and political leadership that benefit from the crisis.

🌍 **The Global Script: The Same Handlers, A Different Theater**

This Polish theater is not unique. Instead, it is a localized performance of a global script that has appeared elsewhere: the destabilization of sovereign nations to impose a new governance model.

· The WEF's Agenda 2030 provides the ideological framework, in which "rule of law" is defined by compliance with supranational bodies rather than national constitutions.

· The same colour revolution playbook is being applied. A disputed legal technicality is escalated into a "constitutional crisis," a "coup" narrative is pushed, and the street is mobilized to create the impression of a legitimacy crisis for the elected government.

· Ultimately, the goal, as presented in this analysis, is not Polish sovereignty but the creation of a managed crisis that justifies deeper integration, centralization of power in Brussels, and the marginalization of any government that puts the nation first.

The Polish people are being used as extras in a drama allegedly designed in Brussels, Berlin and Washington. The "coup" is the plot device, while the march is the scenery. Meanwhile, the real script is the continued transfer of Polish sovereignty to the EU's bureaucratic architecture.

💎 **The Bill**

The bill for this performance is being paid by the Polish people, who are being divided and radicalized to serve a political conflict that benefits neither side. The receipt is a 250,000-person march organized to create the illusion of a massive, unstoppable revolt in a country where 70% of the population still wants to remain in the EU.

The only thing "historic" about November 11, 2026, is the cynicism of the script.

$AMRO Q3 2026 earnings: Amaero's defense backlog nearly triples, but factory losses widen

Amaero, a producer of specialized metal powders and 3D-printed industrial parts, grew orders rapidly while a factory shutdown hurt profitability. Third-quarter revenue rose 35% to $4.1 million, and the twelve-month order backlog nearly tripled to $13.4 million on new U. S. defense work. However, a six-week safety pause in titanium production and slow tuning of new machinery pushed the quarterly net loss to $9.1 million. Chief executive Hank Holland issued a fourth-quarter sales outlook of $4.5 million to $5.0 million.

• Revenue: $𝟒.𝟏𝐌 (+35% from a year ago)
• Gross loss: $𝟒.𝟒𝐌 ($0.1M loss a year ago)
• Order backlog: $𝟏𝟑.𝟒𝐌 (+180% from a year ago)
• Full-year revenue outlook: $𝟏𝟔.𝟎–$𝟏𝟔.𝟓𝐌 (+158% at the middle of the range)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because factory production costs more than doubled as a share of sales and forced costly new financing. To replenish cash after burning $33 million across nine months, the manufacturer diluted shareholders by 21% in an October stock offering and pledged almost all its assets to its lender. On the positive side, submarine component manufacturing moved from development into initial production.

The question now is whether the wide gross loss was a one-off penalty from the summer restart or a sign that factory overhead is too heavy for current order volumes. Either higher fourth-quarter shipments absorb the fixed plant salaries and equipment costs, or low yields keep production unprofitable and drain the new cash buffer. Fourth-quarter gross margin in the full-year report will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐨𝐠
Amaero produces specialized titanium and heat-resistant metal powders for 3D printing. The Tennessee manufacturer relies on U. S. defense and industrial orders to fill its newly expanded factory. In July, the U. S. Department of War awarded the company a $4.5 million contract to develop alternative heat-resistant alloy powders "to reduce cost and dependence on foreign sources of critical raw materials".

• Total backlog: $13.4 million at quarter end, up 180% from $4.8 million a year ago
• Net backlog added: $6.5 million since the end of 2025, an increase of 96%
• Department of War share: $4.4 million of current backlog, or 33% of the total by our math

This backlog matters because legally binding orders expected to ship within twelve months now cover nearly three quarters of the company's full-year sales target. Furthermore, Amaero has already selected and produced two high-temperature alloys on its equipment under the 13-month defense program.

What to watch: fourth-quarter revenue against the $4.5 million to $5.0 million outlook. Delivering that range will show that the plant can turn its record order book into shipments on schedule.

🟢 𝐒𝐮𝐛𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐌𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐈𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧
Alongside loose metal powders, Amaero uses Powder Metallurgy Hot Isostatic Pressing (PM-HIP), a process that fuses metal powder under high heat and pressure into large, near-finished industrial parts. Chief executive Hank Holland said this capability has moved into production for the U. S. submarine industrial base.

In July, the company won a $0.3 million Low-Rate Initial Production (LRIP) contract from Bechtel Plant Machinery, "moving PM-HIP from development into low-rate initial production". That milestone helped push third-quarter component sales up 146% from a year ago to $0.9 million, while powder sales grew 19% to $3.2 million. Because manufactured parts grew seven times faster than powder, components expanded their share of revenue from 12.2% to 22.2% by our math, reducing reliance on a single product.

What to watch: follow-on production orders from Bechtel or other naval contractors over the next two quarters. Repeat commercial orders would prove that initial qualification wins can scale into recurring factory volume.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬
"Our third quarter gross margin was impacted by the restart of titanium production following the pause and the optimization of our new sieving system, which reduced titanium throughput and yields during the quarter," chief executive Hank Holland said. Following safety incidents, the metal producer halted titanium operations for about six weeks to complete a safety review with engineering firm Jensen Hughes before restarting in late July.

In August, the company also installed a custom sieving system and a third furnace that doubled titanium capacity to 480 metric tons a year. However, cost of revenue — the direct cost of making products, including factory labor, equipment depreciation and lease expenses — jumped to $8.5 million, or 206.5% of sales, up 103.5 percentage points of revenue from 103.0% a year ago by our math.

Amaero said it "does not expect these fixed production costs to increase in proportion to revenue" now that its plant teams and machinery are in place. Yet third-quarter revenue rose $1.1 million while cost of revenue rose $5.4 million, so variable waste and unabsorbed factory overhead overwhelmed sales growth and widened the gross loss from $0.1 million to $4.4 million.

What to watch: fourth-quarter gross loss when full-year results arrive. If revenue reaches $4.5 million to $5.0 million without a sharp drop in cost of revenue, the margin problem is ongoing rather than a one-time restart cost.

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐁𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐥𝐞𝐝𝐠𝐞𝐬
Building out the Tennessee manufacturing plant has consumed cash far faster than customer collections have brought it in. Across the first nine months of 2026, Amaero spent $19.2 million in operating cash and $13.9 million on factory equipment, leaving just $5.0 million of unrestricted cash on September 30, down from $31.9 million at the end of 2025.

• October stock offering: 5.0 million new shares sold at $4.25 each, expanding the share count by 21.0% by our math
• Net cash raised: $17.0 million after fees, lifting October 31 unrestricted cash to $19.3 million
• Planned equipment spending: up to $10.0 million of the offering proceeds over the next 12 months

To free up another $2.1 million of restricted cash and push a minimum liquidity test back by one year to September 2028, the company amended its Export-Import Bank credit agreement in October and pledged substantially all of its assets as collateral. Because up to $10.0 million of the new money is earmarked for equipment, the remaining cash buffer leaves little room if operating losses stay near $9.1 million a quarter.

What to watch: quarterly operating cash burn in the full-year report. If cash used in operations does not fall toward the single-digit millions, the company may need additional outside financing in 2027.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐔.𝐒. 𝐌𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐋𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬
Amaero moved its corporate home from Australia to Delaware and listed on Nasdaq in October to align with U. S. defense customers. Legal, tax and audit fees for the move and offering preparation added $0.6 million to third-quarter selling, general and administrative expenses, which rose 14.7% to $4.3 million. Excluding those one-off costs, overhead fell 2.5% from a year ago by our math, helped by $0.5 million in stock-compensation forfeitures.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟖.𝟔𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Unpaid bills to suppliers more than tripled from $2.54 million at the end of 2025, rising 242.3% by our math. Stretching vendor payments provided $3.44 million of operating cash inflow during the first nine months, which helped preserve cash before the October stock offering closed.

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟑.𝟎𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Combined short-term and long-term borrowings rose 54.0% from $14.94 million at year-end 2025 by our math. The titanium powder maker drew $8.14 million in loan proceeds during the first nine months to fund factory equipment, which pushed third-quarter interest expense up from $0.13 million to $0.48 million.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑.𝟖𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Money owed by customers and unbilled contract work nearly tripled from $1.34 million at the end of 2025 by our math. Contract assets — revenue recognized for work performed before the customer is billed — jumped from $10 thousand to $1.01 million, absorbing $2.53 million of cash across the first nine months.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐐𝟒 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟒.𝟓–$𝟓.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. In its first outlook under U. S. accounting rules, the company plans for fourth-quarter sales to rise 121% to 146% from $2.0 million a year ago. By our math, the middle of the range ($4.75 million) represents a 15.5% increase from the third quarter, supported by the return of titanium production after the summer safety pause.

𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐟 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟖.𝟔–$𝟗.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. Combining third-quarter sales of $4.1 million with the fourth-quarter outlook puts second-half revenue up 69% to 79% from $5.1 million in the prior year. By our math, that is an 18.8% increase at the middle of the range over the $7.4 million Amaero generated in the first half of 2026.

𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $𝟏𝟔.𝟎–$𝟏𝟔.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
New. Full-year sales are set to grow 154% to 162% from $6.3 million in 2025. Because the company has already recorded $11.5 million in the first nine months and holds $13.4 million in twelve-month backlog, the remaining fourth-quarter target is well covered by existing contracts.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐢𝐱-𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐤 𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐮𝐦 𝐬𝐚𝐟𝐞𝐭𝐲 𝐬𝐡𝐮𝐭𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧?
The release mentions safety incidents that forced a six-week pause and an engineering review with Jensen Hughes. Investors need to know what went wrong, how much the fixes cost, and whether titanium yields have now returned to normal levels.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬?
Cost of revenue hit $8.5 million on $4.1 million of sales, and management says fixed plant costs are now largely in place. Knowing the exact quarterly revenue required to reach breakeven gross margin is essential for judging the 2027 cash runway.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐡 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧?
Under Australian rules on an earlier fiscal calendar, management targeted $18 million to $20 million in annual sales. Under U. S. rules for calendar 2026, the outlook is $16.0 million to $16.5 million. Management should bridge how much of the gap is calendar timing versus the production pause.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 $𝟖.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐝𝐮𝐞?
Accounts payable jumped by $6.1 million over nine months to $8.7 million. Paying down those overdue vendor balances in the fourth quarter could absorb a large share of the $17.0 million raised in the October stock offering.
